In summary, our research is concerned with
the importance of the introduction of exotic species on the structure of plant assemblage, and how it can affect the functioning of ecosystems.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the introduction of alien plants to the islands of the southeastern Pacific has had a major effect on the composition and phylogenetic structure, and consequently the functioning, of plant assemblage on these islands.
the introduction of non-native species to oceanic islands has been the major cause of change in phylogenetic and functional diversity, and therefore in ecosystem services.
the introduction of invasive species has a greater effect on the configuration of plant phylogenetic diversity than the extinction of native species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the studied islands, exotic plants have contributed more than local extinctions to the current configuration of plant assembalges and their phylogenetic diversity.
, in general, exotic species have contributed more than extinctions to changes of phylogenetic diversity in the angiosperm assembles of the six studied oceanic islands.
the introduction of plants has modified the phylogenetic structure and composition of plant assemblage on these islands.
The main takeaway from our work is that

phylogenetic diversity should be included in conservation planning of oceanic islands, and that exotic plants should be controlled to avoid further changes in phylogenetically diverse plant assemblages.

the phylogenetic structure (i.e., the phylogenetic diversity) of island flora is highly sensitive to changes in the species composition of the community, which in the case of islands is mostly driven by human activities.
phylogenetic diversity, as a measure of biodiversity, should be considered when evaluating conservation priorities and management of plant assemblage on islands.
